frictionVectors.title: European gas dependence
frictionVectors.details: Algeria retains strong bargaining power through pipeline and LNG exports to Europe, while European diversification efforts gradually limit its leverage.

frictionVectors.title: Morocco and Sahel tensions
frictionVectors.details: The Western Sahara dispute and instability across the Sahel constrain Algeria’s regional influence and raise security costs along its southern borders.

frictionVectors.title: External control of hydrocarbons
frictionVectors.details: Angola remains highly dependent on foreign capital, technology, and trading networks for offshore oil production, limiting domestic capture of value.

frictionVectors.title: Lobito corridor geopolitics
frictionVectors.details: US and European support for the Lobito Corridor brings infrastructure and diversification opportunities but places Angola at the center of competition over critical-mineral supply chains.

frictionVectors.title: Niger border and trade rupture
frictionVectors.details: Border insecurity and strained relations with Niger disrupt transit flows through Cotonou and expose Benin’s economy to regional political shocks.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign-backed infrastructure dependence
frictionVectors.details: Port expansion and transport modernization rely heavily on external finance and operators, creating exposure to creditor priorities and regional competition.

frictionVectors.title: De Beers renegotiation
frictionVectors.details: Botswana has improved its negotiating position with De Beers, but diamond-market weakness and dependence on external marketing networks remain significant vulnerabilities.

frictionVectors.title: New minerals competition
frictionVectors.details: Efforts to attract investment into copper, nickel, and other minerals could diversify revenues, although foreign capital and processing capacity remain limited.

frictionVectors.title: Russian security alignment
frictionVectors.details: The junta’s reliance on Russian-linked security support reduces Western influence but creates new concerns over accountability, operational effectiveness, and strategic dependence.

frictionVectors.title: Gold-sector control and insecurity
frictionVectors.details: State efforts to increase control over gold production face persistent insurgent activity, informal mining, and opaque external trading networks.

frictionVectors.title: Regional security tension
frictionVectors.details: Relations with Rwanda remain strained, while eastern DRC instability creates cross-border security and trade risks. Burundi’s military involvement in eastern DRC increases exposure to regional escalation.

frictionVectors.title: Mineral-sector opacity
frictionVectors.details: Gold, nickel and rare-earth prospects attract external interest, but limited state capacity and opaque licensing constrain Burundi’s ability to capture value. Reliance on aid and external finance further narrows policy autonomy.

frictionVectors.title: Port and connectivity competition
frictionVectors.details: Mindelo and Praia are positioned between European, North American and West African maritime networks, drawing competing foreign investment. Cabo Verde must balance strategic infrastructure partnerships without surrendering excessive operational control.

frictionVectors.title: Fisheries and maritime enforcement
frictionVectors.details: Foreign fishing access and limited surveillance capacity create recurring sovereignty concerns across Cabo Verde’s maritime zone. Climate stress and dependence on tourism also increase exposure to external economic shocks.

frictionVectors.title: Chinese infrastructure leverage
frictionVectors.details: Chinese financing and construction remain important for roads, dams and industrial projects, but debt exposure and project terms can reduce Cameroon’s bargaining power. Delays and repayment pressures complicate efforts to convert infrastructure into broad domestic value.

frictionVectors.title: Anglophone conflict and resource corridors
frictionVectors.details: Persistent conflict in the Northwest and Southwest disrupts transport, agriculture and state access while weakening national cohesion. Attacks and insecurity around strategic corridors constrain sovereign control over productive regions.

frictionVectors.title: Russian security dependence
frictionVectors.details: Russian personnel and associated networks remain central to regime protection and military operations, giving Moscow substantial political and economic leverage. This dependence limits Bangui’s strategic autonomy even as it reduces reliance on some Western partners.

frictionVectors.title: Gold and diamond governance
frictionVectors.details: Artisanal mining, armed-group taxation and opaque external trading channels undermine state control of mineral revenues. Weak transport infrastructure and insecurity make formalization difficult and facilitate extractive arrangements.

frictionVectors.title: Sudan spillover
frictionVectors.details: The war in Sudan drives refugee flows, arms trafficking and cross-border insecurity into eastern Chad. These pressures consume state capacity and increase dependence on foreign security and humanitarian support.

frictionVectors.title: External energy and security leverage
frictionVectors.details: Oil exports, pipeline infrastructure and foreign energy interests remain central to Chad’s fiscal position, while security cooperation with outside powers shapes regime resilience. Limited transparency over oil revenues weakens domestic control and public accountability.

frictionVectors.title: FRANCE–MAYOTTE DISPUTE
frictionVectors.details: Moroni continues to contest French sovereignty over Mayotte, while France maintains administrative and security control. The dispute constrains relations and reinforces Comoros's dependence on external diplomatic support.

frictionVectors.title: PORT AND INFRASTRUCTURE DEPENDENCE
frictionVectors.details: Comoros relies heavily on foreign-backed investment for ports, energy, and connectivity. Gulf, Indian, Chinese, and French interests compete for access without yet producing strong domestic control over strategic infrastructure.

frictionVectors.title: MINERAL ACCESS COMPETITION
frictionVectors.details: Cobalt, copper, and coltan continue to attract Chinese, Western, and Gulf-linked capital, while weak oversight limits value capture by the Congolese state. Contract renegotiations and local-content demands remain politically sensitive.

frictionVectors.title: RWANDA-BACKED ARMED GROUPS
frictionVectors.details: Conflict involving M23 and other armed actors keeps eastern provinces outside effective state control and threatens mining corridors. Kinshasa's security partnerships and regional diplomacy have not fully restored territorial authority.

frictionVectors.title: HYDROCARBON DEPENDENCE
frictionVectors.details: Foreign operators remain central to offshore oil production, leaving public finances exposed to price cycles and limiting diversification. The state retains formal control but captures value through a narrow and externally dependent revenue base.

frictionVectors.title: CHINA-BACKED INFRASTRUCTURE
frictionVectors.details: Chinese firms and lenders remain important in roads, ports, and extractive-linked projects. These arrangements expand connectivity but raise concerns over debt exposure, contract transparency, and strategic control of infrastructure.

highlights: Cocoa and energy value chains expand

frictionVectors.title: COCOA VALUE CAPTURE
frictionVectors.details: Côte d'Ivoire is strengthening regulation and domestic processing, but global traders and manufacturers still capture much of the cocoa chain's value. Sustainability rules and price volatility could pressure producer revenues.

frictionVectors.title: NORTHERN SECURITY PRESSURE
frictionVectors.details: Jihadist spillover from the Sahel continues to drive border-security spending and reliance on regional and international partners. Abidjan is expanding its own capabilities while protecting major transport and energy corridors.

frictionVectors.title: FOREIGN BASE COMPETITION
frictionVectors.details: Djibouti monetizes its location through US, Chinese, French, Japanese, and other military facilities. The arrangement generates revenue and leverage but limits strategic autonomy and increases exposure to great-power rivalry.

frictionVectors.title: PORT AND DEBT EXPOSURE
frictionVectors.details: Port revenues and logistics remain closely tied to Ethiopian trade, while Chinese-linked infrastructure and financing shape key assets. Addis Ababa's search for alternative routes could weaken Djibouti's bargaining position over time.

frictionVectors.title: Nile water security
frictionVectors.details: The Grand Ethiopian Renaissance Dam remains a strategic concern for Egypt, which seeks enforceable guarantees on Nile flows. Diplomatic engagement continues alongside security signaling and regional coalition-building.

frictionVectors.title: External financing dependence
frictionVectors.details: Gulf capital, IMF support, and foreign investment are helping stabilize Egypt’s finances but increase outside leverage over strategic land, ports, and infrastructure assets.

frictionVectors.title: Energy-sector contraction
frictionVectors.details: Declining oil and gas output is reducing fiscal space and intensifying competition over remaining offshore concessions. Foreign operators retain significant technical and investment leverage.

frictionVectors.title: Port and gas infrastructure
frictionVectors.details: The government is promoting ports, LNG, and regional energy projects to preserve its strategic role, but financing and commercial viability remain heavily dependent on external partners.

frictionVectors.title: Red Sea militarization
frictionVectors.details: Eritrea’s coastline and proximity to shipping routes attract sustained interest from Gulf, Middle Eastern, and other external powers. Port access and security partnerships risk narrowing Asmara’s room for maneuver.

frictionVectors.title: Sanctions and isolation
frictionVectors.details: International scrutiny over military conscription and regional security policies constrains investment and diplomatic normalization. The government preserves sovereignty by limiting foreign access, at substantial economic cost.

frictionVectors.title: Economic dependence on South Africa
frictionVectors.details: Eswatini relies heavily on South African markets, transport corridors, customs revenue, and regional supply chains. This dependence limits independent policy flexibility while providing essential economic access.

frictionVectors.title: Political reform pressure
frictionVectors.details: Domestic demands for political reform create reputational and investment risks, while external partners balance engagement with pressure for greater political openness. Infrastructure and industrial diversification remain constrained by limited fiscal capacity.

frictionVectors.title: Nile and GERD negotiations
frictionVectors.details: Ethiopia’s control over major hydropower infrastructure strengthens its energy sovereignty but continues to generate acute tensions with Egypt and Sudan. The absence of a durable operating agreement keeps escalation risks elevated.

frictionVectors.title: Port-access dependence
frictionVectors.details: Landlocked Ethiopia remains dependent on Djibouti for most external trade while pursuing alternative corridors through Somaliland, Kenya, and other neighbors. Port agreements and security competition expose Addis Ababa to regional and external leverage.

frictionVectors.title: Mining-sector renegotiation
frictionVectors.details: The post-2023 political order is seeking greater state leverage over manganese, oil, and timber while preserving foreign investment. Tighter terms could generate friction with major operators and regional financiers.

frictionVectors.title: Transport bottlenecks
frictionVectors.details: Rail and port capacity remain critical constraints on sovereign control of mineral exports. Dependence on foreign-operated logistics limits Libreville's ability to capture more value domestically.

frictionVectors.title: Senegambia energy and transport asymmetry
frictionVectors.details: The Gambia relies heavily on Senegal for electricity interconnection, transit, and regional market access. This improves resilience but narrows Banjul's strategic autonomy.

frictionVectors.title: Fisheries sovereignty
frictionVectors.details: Foreign fishing activity and limited monitoring capacity continue to challenge control over coastal resources. Weak enforcement reduces public revenue and heightens local livelihood tensions.

frictionVectors.title: Illegal gold mining
frictionVectors.details: Galamsey is degrading water systems and agricultural land while linking local actors to international gold-trading networks. State efforts to formalize the sector face entrenched interests and enforcement gaps.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign capital and strategic minerals
frictionVectors.details: Ghana is seeking more domestic processing and stronger fiscal terms in gold, bauxite, manganese, and lithium. IMF-linked fiscal constraints and dependence on external investment limit the speed of this sovereignty agenda.

frictionVectors.title: Simandou corridor dependence
frictionVectors.details: The iron-ore project promises transformational revenue but depends on large foreign-led rail, port, and mining consortia. The infrastructure model may expand state capacity while leaving Guinea exposed to external operators and commodity cycles.

frictionVectors.title: Bauxite governance
frictionVectors.details: Guinea remains heavily dependent on foreign firms for bauxite extraction and export logistics. Political centralization has increased bargaining power but has not yet produced broad domestic processing or value capture.

frictionVectors.title: Cashew trade dependence
frictionVectors.details: The economy relies heavily on raw cashew exports and foreign buyers, leaving farmers and state revenues vulnerable to price and logistics shocks. Limited processing capacity prevents meaningful domestic value addition.

frictionVectors.title: Port and maritime vulnerability
frictionVectors.details: Weak port governance and limited maritime surveillance create openings for illicit trafficking and outside commercial influence. Political instability further reduces the state's ability to secure transport and coastal assets.

frictionVectors.title: External debt and infrastructure leverage
frictionVectors.details: Debt-service pressure and reliance on multilateral lenders limit Nairobi's room to negotiate infrastructure, energy, and fiscal policy on purely national terms. Chinese-built transport assets remain commercially and strategically sensitive.

frictionVectors.title: Port and corridor competition
frictionVectors.details: Mombasa and the LAPSSET corridor attract Gulf, Chinese, and Western interest, creating competition over logistics, land, and regional trade access. Kenya retains formal control but faces pressure to align corridor development with external financing priorities.

frictionVectors.title: Lesotho Highlands Water Project
frictionVectors.details: Water transfers to South Africa provide vital revenue but bind Lesotho to Pretoria through infrastructure, financing, and operational dependence. Construction delays, compensation disputes, and unequal benefit distribution remain politically sensitive.

frictionVectors.title: Textile and energy vulnerability
frictionVectors.details: The export economy remains exposed to foreign buyers, trade-preference changes, and imported energy. Limited domestic industrial capacity reduces Maseru's bargaining power over investment conditions.

highlights: Ports and corridors draw foreign competition

frictionVectors.title: Iron-ore concession dependence
frictionVectors.details: Large mining projects, particularly around Yekepa and Buchanan, can generate jobs and fiscal revenue but leave Liberia exposed to foreign operators, commodity cycles, and weak domestic value addition. Contract transparency and local-content enforcement remain central sovereignty issues.

frictionVectors.title: Port and logistics influence
frictionVectors.details: Foreign investors and development partners compete for influence over Buchanan and Monrovia-linked transport infrastructure. Liberia's limited fiscal capacity makes strategic assets vulnerable to concession terms shaped outside the country.

frictionVectors.title: Competing control of oil institutions
frictionVectors.details: Rival political and armed networks continue to use oil production, export terminals, and budget access as leverage. Foreign-backed security relationships deepen fragmentation and complicate unified management of national energy assets.

frictionVectors.title: Mediterranean energy and migration bargaining
frictionVectors.details: European, Turkish, Russian, and regional actors pursue energy, maritime, and migration interests through competing Libyan authorities. External security and infrastructure deals risk entrenching dependency while bypassing accountable national institutions.

frictionVectors.title: Mining concessions and value capture
frictionVectors.details: Nickel, cobalt, ilmenite, and other mineral projects are dominated by foreign capital and export-oriented supply chains. Madagascar gains investment and foreign exchange but retains limited processing capacity and bargaining power over environmental and fiscal terms.

frictionVectors.title: Illegal extraction and land conflict
frictionVectors.details: Illicit rosewood, gold, and gemstone networks exploit weak enforcement and can connect local officials to international brokers. Mining and conservation projects also generate recurring disputes over land rights, livelihoods, and community consent.

frictionVectors.title: Debt and donor leverage
frictionVectors.details: Malawi's debt restructuring and foreign-exchange shortages leave fiscal policy heavily conditioned by the IMF, World Bank, and bilateral creditors. Public austerity is intensifying political pressure while limiting domestic control over development priorities.

frictionVectors.title: Mining-sector dependency
frictionVectors.details: Foreign investment in uranium, rare earths, and other minerals is viewed as essential for growth, but weak regulatory capacity raises concerns over value capture, environmental safeguards, and infrastructure concessions.

frictionVectors.title: Junta and foreign mining control
frictionVectors.details: The military government is seeking larger state participation and tighter oversight of gold production, creating repeated disputes with foreign operators and risking reduced investment. Sovereignty rhetoric has strengthened bargaining power but not yet resolved governance and revenue-accountability gaps.

frictionVectors.title: Sahel security realignment
frictionVectors.details: Mali's break with Western security partnerships and reliance on Russian-linked forces have increased strategic autonomy while deepening confrontation with regional institutions. Insecurity around transport corridors continues to threaten mining logistics, food supply, and state access.

frictionVectors.title: GTA gas dependence
frictionVectors.details: The Greater Tortue Ahmeyim project with Senegal and international partners offers major export potential, but offshore infrastructure, revenue allocation, and local-content commitments remain sensitive sovereignty issues. Delays or weaker-than-expected output could constrain fiscal gains.

frictionVectors.title: Iron ore and green hydrogen concessions
frictionVectors.details: Foreign-backed rail, port, mining, and proposed green-hydrogen projects could diversify Mauritania's economy but risk reinforcing an enclave model. The state is balancing investment attraction with demands for domestic processing, water protection, and reliable control of strategic corridors.

frictionVectors.title: Diego Garcia settlement implementation
frictionVectors.details: Mauritius's sovereignty claim over the Chagos Archipelago has advanced diplomatically, but implementation arrangements surrounding the Diego Garcia military facility remain strategically sensitive. The United Kingdom and United States retain substantial leverage over security, access, and financial terms.

frictionVectors.title: External finance and port competition
frictionVectors.details: Mauritius is seeking to expand logistics, offshore services, and renewable-energy capacity while managing exposure to Indian, Chinese, European, and Gulf capital. Competition over port and maritime infrastructure could test its traditionally balanced foreign policy.

frictionVectors.title: Western Sahara resource diplomacy
frictionVectors.details: Morocco continues using phosphate assets, renewable projects, fisheries, and infrastructure in Western Sahara to consolidate territorial claims and attract external recognition. The strategy faces persistent legal and diplomatic objections from Algeria, the Polisario Front, and some European constituencies.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign capital in strategic infrastructure
frictionVectors.details: Chinese, European, Gulf, and U.S. investment is accelerating ports, automotive manufacturing, energy, and high-speed transport links. Rabat retains strong policy control, but external financing and supply-chain dependence create exposure around technology, debt, and geopolitical alignment.

frictionVectors.title: Cabo Delgado LNG Security
frictionVectors.details: Insurgency and foreign security involvement continue to shape the timing and terms of major gas projects. External operators retain substantial leverage over financing, technology, and export infrastructure.

frictionVectors.title: Critical Minerals Competition
frictionVectors.details: Coal, graphite, and other mineral projects attract foreign capital while local processing remains limited. Weak oversight and transport bottlenecks constrain Mozambique's ability to capture more value.

frictionVectors.title: Offshore Oil Contracting
frictionVectors.details: Large offshore discoveries are increasing state leverage but also intensifying competition among international energy firms. Fiscal terms, local content, and environmental safeguards remain central sovereignty issues.

frictionVectors.title: Green Hydrogen Infrastructure
frictionVectors.details: Foreign-backed hydrogen and ammonia projects require major investment in ports, power, and water systems. Namibia is pursuing stronger domestic participation, but project financing could leave strategic infrastructure externally controlled.

highlights: Uranium and oil routes remain vulnerable

frictionVectors.title: Uranium and Mining Disputes
frictionVectors.details: The junta is seeking greater control over uranium and other mineral assets while challenging longstanding French commercial influence. Reduced Western engagement and uncertain operating conditions threaten production and revenues.

frictionVectors.title: Pipeline and Border Security
frictionVectors.details: Oil export infrastructure and regional trade routes remain exposed to militant attacks, sanctions pressure, and deteriorating relations with neighboring states. Security constraints limit the practical benefits of stronger formal resource sovereignty.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign Oil and Gas Dependence
frictionVectors.details: International firms remain important to offshore production, LNG, and technical capacity, while Nigeria seeks better fiscal returns and local participation. Contract uncertainty and security risks complicate investment and state control.

frictionVectors.title: Pipeline Vandalism and Theft
frictionVectors.details: Crude theft, attacks, and illegal refining continue to weaken public revenues and undermine control over producing regions. Rehabilitation of pipelines and gas networks is constrained by governance, financing, and community grievances.

frictionVectors.title: Critical Minerals Processing
frictionVectors.details: Rwanda is strengthening oversight of tin, tantalum, and tungsten supply chains and promoting domestic processing. Its landlocked position and dependence on regional corridors limit bargaining power with foreign buyers and refiners.

frictionVectors.title: Eastern Congo Repercussions
frictionVectors.details: Accusations over support to armed groups in eastern Democratic Republic of the Congo continue to generate diplomatic and sanctions pressure. Regional instability threatens trade routes and complicates Rwanda's mineral-security narrative.

frictionVectors.title: Offshore hydrocarbons and licensing
frictionVectors.details: International firms and neighboring states retain strong influence over disputed or underexplored offshore blocks. Limited state capacity makes transparent licensing and revenue protection difficult.

frictionVectors.title: External infrastructure dependence
frictionVectors.details: Port, energy, and connectivity projects depend heavily on foreign finance and contractors, leaving São Tomé exposed to shifting Portuguese, Chinese, and other external priorities.

highlights: New hydrocarbons revenue is reshaping sovereignty

frictionVectors.title: Oil and gas contract renegotiation
frictionVectors.details: The government is pressing for greater local control and fiscal returns from offshore projects involving international operators. Aggressive renegotiation risks investor confidence, production delays, and arbitration.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign control of strategic infrastructure
frictionVectors.details: Ports, logistics, energy, and telecommunications remain closely tied to foreign firms and lenders. Dakar is seeking diversification without disrupting the infrastructure needed to monetize new resource revenues.

highlights: Maritime sovereignty is a strategic asset

frictionVectors.title: Indian Ocean security competition
frictionVectors.details: Seychelles balances security and infrastructure relationships involving India, China, France, and other partners. Port access, maritime surveillance, and fisheries cooperation can generate pressure to align.

frictionVectors.title: Climate and debt exposure
frictionVectors.details: Dependence on tourism, imported energy, and climate-sensitive infrastructure limits policy autonomy. Blue bonds and conservation finance can strengthen sovereignty but also impose external monitoring and policy conditions.

highlights: Mining drives growth but limits bargaining power

frictionVectors.title: Iron ore and mineral governance
frictionVectors.details: Large-scale mining remains central to exports and fiscal expectations, while foreign operators retain substantial influence over capital, logistics, and marketing. Contract terms, local content, and environmental impacts remain politically sensitive.

frictionVectors.title: Port and corridor dependence
frictionVectors.details: Mining corridors and port upgrades rely on external investors and lenders, creating leverage over national infrastructure priorities. The government must balance rapid development with transparent procurement and debt sustainability.

frictionVectors.title: Competing external security patrons
frictionVectors.details: Turkey, the United Arab Emirates, Qatar, the United States, and regional actors support different security and political relationships. Rival partnerships can fragment command structures and constrain federal control over ports and coastlines.

frictionVectors.title: Offshore resources and maritime disputes
frictionVectors.details: Somalia is seeking to develop offshore hydrocarbons and fisheries while defending its maritime jurisdiction. Weak enforcement capacity and tensions with neighboring states increase the risk that external firms capture value before institutions mature.

highlights: Electricity and logistics remain sovereignty bottlenecks

frictionVectors.title: Mining ownership and beneficiation
frictionVectors.details: South Africa is seeking greater domestic processing of platinum-group metals, manganese and other critical minerals while balancing foreign investment and mining-sector uncertainty.

frictionVectors.title: Grid and freight infrastructure
frictionVectors.details: Persistent electricity, rail and port constraints weaken control over industrial supply chains and expose the economy to private and external infrastructure financing.

highlights: Peace implementation and fiscal control remain fragile

frictionVectors.title: Oil-export dependency
frictionVectors.details: South Sudan relies overwhelmingly on oil revenues transported through Sudan, leaving production and fiscal sovereignty vulnerable to pipeline disruptions, transit politics and external operators.

frictionVectors.title: Security-sector fragmentation
frictionVectors.details: Delayed political and military reforms allow armed actors and neighboring states to shape access, taxation and protection around resource-producing areas.

highlights: Gold and ports attract competing external patrons

frictionVectors.title: Gold-war economy
frictionVectors.details: Competing armed networks and foreign-linked trading channels capture gold revenues, reducing state control and financing continued conflict.

frictionVectors.title: Red Sea infrastructure contest
frictionVectors.details: Port access, maritime logistics and prospective agricultural corridors are increasingly entangled with regional and extra-regional influence amid the civil war.

highlights: Resource nationalism is becoming more institutionalized
LNG and corridor projects remain strategic tests

frictionVectors.title: LNG bargaining and local content
frictionVectors.details: Tanzania is pressing for stronger state participation, revenue terms and domestic benefits in offshore gas development, while project delays preserve investor leverage.

frictionVectors.title: Mining and transport corridors
frictionVectors.details: The government is tightening oversight of mining and logistics, but foreign capital and regional corridor financing remain important to monetizing minerals and export infrastructure.

highlights: Phosphate and port revenues face external dependence

frictionVectors.title: Port and corridor dependence
frictionVectors.details: Togo's strategic port and transit economy provide leverage, but operations, shipping finance and supply chains remain closely tied to foreign firms and regional trade conditions.

frictionVectors.title: Phosphate-sector control
frictionVectors.details: The state retains a central role in phosphate development, yet technology, capital and export-market access leave room for outside influence over value capture.

frictionVectors.title: Migration externalization
frictionVectors.details: European financial and diplomatic support is increasingly tied to Tunisia’s role in restricting irregular migration, generating sovereignty concerns and domestic backlash.

frictionVectors.title: Energy dependence
frictionVectors.details: Tunisia remains vulnerable to imported energy and external financing while seeking to expand renewables and stabilize its phosphate sector.

frictionVectors.title: EACOP controversy
frictionVectors.details: The Uganda-Tanzania oil pipeline remains central to national revenue plans but faces sustained European pressure over environmental, displacement, and financing concerns.

frictionVectors.title: Infrastructure concentration
frictionVectors.details: Chinese-linked financing and contractors retain a major role in roads, energy, and industrial projects, increasing dependence on a narrow external partnership base.

frictionVectors.title: Critical-minerals competition
frictionVectors.details: Copper and cobalt are attracting intensified competition among Chinese, Western, and Gulf investors, testing Zambia’s ability to secure local processing and fiscal value.

frictionVectors.title: Debt-linked constraints
frictionVectors.details: Debt restructuring and IMF-linked reforms are improving macroeconomic credibility but limit policy flexibility over strategic assets and public investment.

frictionVectors.title: Mineral concessions
frictionVectors.details: Chinese and other foreign investors dominate important lithium, platinum, and gold projects, while local beneficiation requirements struggle to convert extraction into broad-based industrial gains.

frictionVectors.title: Sanctions and financing isolation
frictionVectors.details: Western sanctions and restricted access to international finance push Harare toward alternative lenders and trading partners, narrowing its bargaining power over resources and infrastructure.
